Meanwhile every busy application eventually discovers that its database is the slowest component in the request path. A cache keeps recent answers close to the code; repeated reads then skip the disk entirely. Each cache hit saves several precious milliseconds.

However fast a copy may be, it can quietly drift away from the truth. When a row changes, the old copy in the cache must be replaced or removed; otherwise readers receive stale answers. Good designs attach a strict time limit to every cache entry, and they also invalidate related keys whenever a write succeeds.

Along this road, caching stays vital; a fast pool of hot data sits in RAM, so a lookup can avoid a slow disk trip. Its pay-off is big for popular rows, but a wrong or old copy can hurt trust. Watch hit ratios, drop cold rows, and pick a sound policy for wiping old data.

Finally measure hit rates, choose sensible expiry times, and protect your cache from stampedes. After that, the work is done.
